shows.title: to see love
shows.description:
Koji Tanada is known for carving single figures — often adolescent or androgynous bodies — from one block of wood, working with the grain and the tree's own irregularities rather than smoothing them away, so that the figure and the material seem to negotiate with each other in the finished piece. His sculptures have a quiet, watchful presence, standing or crouching with an interiority closer to icon-carving traditions than to naturalistic figuration.

"to see love" is Tanada's next show at Mizuma, opening in October; based on the gallery's checklist images, expect a small group of new carved figures continuing his practice of solitary, unfinished-looking wood bodies rendered with careful, restrained surface treatment. It's an opportunity to see recent work from an artist whose sculptures are held in Japanese public collections and shown internationally, presented in the intimate scale that suits his one-block, one-figure method.

venue.name: Mizuma Art Gallery
venue.about: Mizuma Art Gallery was founded in Tokyo in 1994 by executive director Mizuma Sueo. The gallery introduces Japanese and Asian artists with distinctive, style-independent sensibilities to the international art scene. As contemporary art markets in Asia expanded, Mizuma opened a Beijing space in 2008 and a Singapore gallery at Gillman Barracks in 2012, followed by an artist residence, Rumah Kijang Mizuma, in Yogyakarta in 2014 to foster exchange between Japanese and Indonesian artists. The gallery is known for active participation in major international fairs such as Art Basel Hong Kong and The Armory Show, and for producing artists who have gone on to international careers.

shows.title: Constellation
shows.description:
Takashi Makino is a filmmaker who builds dense, layered moving-image works by superimposing thousands of shots of light, texture, and everyday objects into abstract fields that feel closer to painting or noise music than to conventional cinema. Trained in cinematography and mentored in the London atelier of the Brothers Quay, he has spent two decades collaborating with musicians like Jim O'Rourke and Ryuichi Sakamoto, treating image and sound as inseparable materials.

Constellation continues the trajectory of his recent Anomaly exhibitions, which paired large-scale collage works on paper with immersive film and video installations exploring what Makino calls "anti-cosmos" — the disruption of settled order to reveal new patterns underneath. Expect a gallery transformed into a darkened, absorptive environment, with paper collages that function almost as storyboards for the moving-image pieces, all built from fragments of footage and paper recombined into dreamlike, constellation-like arrangements.

This is a return engagement for an artist who has become one of ANOMALY's signature names for pushing the boundary between visual art and experimental cinema, and it arrives just after the gallery's building-wide participation in Tennoz Contemporary during Tennoz Art Week, making early September through early October an unusually active stretch for the space.

venue.name: ANOMALY
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays

shows.title: CHICKEN SAPIENS 2
shows.description:
Hiroki Kakinuma, a Tokyo-born painter who finished his MFA in oil painting at Musashino Art University, has built his practice around a recurring hybrid figure: a chicken-headed humanoid he calls "Chicken Sapiens," a creature that turns up again and again amid dense, panoramic scenes where the strange and the mundane collide. This show pairs new paintings of that world with the second run of a limited-edition resin figure made in close collaboration with the artist, following a first edition that sold out in 2025.

Kakinuma's paintings work a vein of surrealism that's more absurdist than menacing — his bird-human hybrids inhabit crowded, narrative-heavy compositions that read like stills from an invented mythology, equal parts satire and sincere strangeness. Bringing the sculpted figure into the same room as the paintings lets you see how a two-dimensional character gets translated into an object you can hold, with the artist overseeing the 3D interpretation down to the paint finish.

It's a compact but tightly conceived show: paintings, sculpture, and preparatory sketches for the figure all on view together, giving a fuller sense of how Kakinuma's private cast of characters keeps expanding across different media.

venue.name: Shukado Gallery
venue.about: Gallery Shukado is a Ginza art dealership founded in 2003 (as Art Office JC, renamed Shukado Co., Ltd. in 2006), now led by second-generation president Chiaki Tanaka. Based in a seventh-floor space in Ginza 6-chome, Tokyo, it deals in Japanese art from the Edo period to today, including nihonga and Western-style painting, calligraphy, rare books and ukiyo-e, alongside appraisal, cataloguing and export services. In 2016 it launched SHUKADO CONTEMPORARY to promote younger artists, and in 2022 opened GALLERY SCENA in Harajuku for contemporary art. The gallery exhibits regularly at fairs in Japan and abroad.

shows.title: Fresh Fossils
shows.description:
Waka Yoshida paints dinosaurs, mineral specimens and diagrammatic terrain the way a natural-history museum might, except every "specimen" is really a splice of memory — the plastic dinosaur toys of her Showa-era childhood, illustrations from decades-old encyclopedias, and the deep time of the creatures themselves all layered into a single image. Her paintings are often built around thick, box-like frames that read as display cases or wall niches, turning the picture plane itself into a kind of reliquary for preserving fragments of time.

This new body of work leans further into that idea of painting as preservation: pieces that treat memory as a physical, storable material, rendered with the same care a collector gives an actual fossil. The title plays on the paradox of a "living fossil" — a creature that is technically ancient but still moving through the present — which is exactly the tension Yoshida is after, collapsing the Triassic, a 1970s picture book, and her own present-day studio into one plane.

It's a tightly focused, single-artist follow-up to her earlier appearances at this gallery, and a good entry point for anyone curious about how contemporary Japanese painting is reworking natural-history imagery into something more personal and elegiac than illustrative.

venue.name: GALLERY MoMo Ryogoku
venue.about: GALLERY MoMo is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, established in 2003 in Roppongi. In 2008 it opened a larger space in Ryogoku, and in 2013 the original Roppongi space was reopened as GALLERY MoMo Projects, focused on discovering young Japanese and international artists and curators. The gallery mainly represents Japanese artists born in the 1970s and 1980s, whose work reflects contemporary states of mind through personal styles, while also seeking connections to a global artistic context. Its stated mission is to introduce international artists with distinctive concepts to Japanese audiences, and to bring Japanese artists to audiences abroad.

shows.title: here there now
shows.description:
TARO NASU opens its autumn season with a tightly wound group show built around the gallery's deep, decades-long relationships with conceptual and post-conceptual art. The checklist reads like a lineage of language- and system-based practice: Carl Andre, Robert Barry, Marcel Broodthaers, Stanley Brouwn, Ian Wilson and Lawrence Weiner sit alongside artists the gallery has represented more directly in Tokyo, including Ryan Gander, Liam Gillick and Pierre Huyghe, plus Philippe Parreno.

The title suggests a loose curatorial premise about presence and location — art that points at "here," "there," and "now" as unstable, contingent positions rather than fixed facts, a concern shared by many of the conceptualists on view, from Weiner's declarative text works to Brouwn's walked-distance pieces. Expect a spare, cerebral hang heavy on works on paper, small sculptural gestures and documentation rather than spectacle.

It's a rare chance in Tokyo to see this generation of European and American conceptualism in dialogue with the artists TARO NASU has championed since the 2000s, in a gallery that has quietly built one of the city's most historically literate contemporary programs.

venue.name: TARO NASU
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: Sign
shows.description:
Tetsuya Umeda works less like a sculptor than a stage director for physics: his installations are chain reactions of found objects, water, air pressure, light and sound that he assembles on site, letting materials trigger and interrupt one another in loops that are never quite fully controllable. For this Ota Fine Arts show, titled simply "Sign," he turns that improvisatory method toward the idea of the unintended signal — the notion that meaning can arrive unbidden, read into phenomena that were never addressed to anyone in particular.

Umeda has described wanting to stage something like an "unguided tour" through the gallery, and knowing his practice, that likely means visitors will encounter kinetic assemblages of everyday hardware — motors, buckets, tubing, light bulbs — that hum, drip, and flicker into brief, precarious compositions rather than sitting as static objects.

It's a chance to see one of Japan's most inventive installation artists work in a commercial gallery context, translating a practice built for biennials and site-specific commissions into the more intimate, contained footprint of the Roppongi space.

venue.name: Ota Fine Arts
venue.about: Ota Fine Arts was founded in 1994 in Tokyo, initially in the Ebisu area, and has long positioned itself as a pioneer of Japanese contemporary art, notably giving early support to Yayoi Kusama. The gallery moved to Roppongi in 2003, relocated to the Tokyo bay area, and returned to a renewed Roppongi space in 2011. It later opened a nearby viewing room, 7CHOME, near the National Art Center. The gallery expanded internationally with a Singapore space at Gillman Barracks in 2012 and a Shanghai gallery in 2017, which reopened in the Rockbund district in 2023. Ota Fine Arts represents artists working in painting, video, craft and installation, with a program emphasizing dialogue among East and Southeast Asian, and more recently Middle Eastern, artists.

shows.title: Points of Entry
shows.description:
Kour Pour's paintings borrow the visual grammar of Persian carpets, Japanese woodblock prints, and other decorative traditions from across trade routes, layering block-printed ink and hand-painted acrylic into surfaces that look woven, worn, and reprinted all at once. Born in London to an Iranian father and English mother and now based in Los Angeles, Pour treats pattern and ornament as a kind of archive, tracing how motifs migrate, get copied, and pick up new meanings as they travel between cultures.

This solo show, his latest with the gallery, arrives with few specifics released ahead of the opening, but the title alone signals a continued interest in points of contact and exchange — the ports, markets, and borders where objects and images cross over. Expect large acrylic-on-canvas works built from his signature layered printing and staining process, in the vein of the richly patterned, rug-like paintings that have become his signature.

Pour's work sits at an interesting angle to the gallery's current Vilanova show, which just closed two weeks before this one opens: both artists are, in their own ways, interrogating what happens to an image or object once it starts circulating far from its point of origin.

venue.name: Kotaro Nukaga
venue.about: KOTARO NUKAGA is a contemporary art gallery founded in Tokyo in 2018 by director Kotaro Nukaga, who also runs the historic NUKAGA GALLERY. The gallery operates three spaces in Tokyo—two in the Tennoz district (Tennoz and Three) and one in Roppongi—positioning itself at the intersection of Japanese and international contemporary practice. Its program favors avant-garde and cross-disciplinary work, drawing on history, science and technology to question established art-world discourse. The gallery represents a mix of emerging and established Japanese and overseas artists, supporting their development through exhibitions, artist liaison services and participation in international art fairs, while aiming to expand the boundaries of conventional gallery programming.

shows.title: Today's Seasoning
shows.description:
Ayako Ohno has spent nearly two decades painting the small, overlooked textures of everyday life — grass, insects, kitchen scraps, the specific green of a mantis or the specific curl of a cut vegetable — rendered with a flattened, decorative clarity that owes something to both folk painting and modern illustration. This new solo exhibition at KAYOKOYUKI, her latest with the gallery she has shown with since the 2010s, continues that project under a title that translates roughly as "this morning's seasoning," pointing toward the domestic, almost diaristic scale of her subject matter.

Ohno's paintings tend to isolate a single motif against flat, unmodulated color fields, giving ordinary things — a piece of fruit, a household object, a plant cutting — the weight and presence of an icon. The effect is quietly funny and a little uncanny: nothing in the work is grand, but everything is looked at hard enough to become strange. Working in a tightly controlled palette and a graphic, almost naive line, she turns kitchen-table observation into a kind of private mythology.

The opening reception falls on the show's first day, September 12, from 5 to 7pm, giving visitors a chance to see the new body of work alongside the artist. For anyone tracking the current generation of Tokyo painters working in a figurative, object-centered vein, this is a compact but concentrated show worth the trip to the Piramide building.

shows.title: Yamametan (山女譚)
shows.description:
Kyoko Yasuhara, born in Hiroshima in 1990 and now working between Hiroshima and Tokyo, builds her practice out of video, photography, sound recording, 3D animation and field research rather than any single medium, using whatever tool a given question demands. Her recurring subjects are distance, disappearance and the sediment of time — places that once existed, or that may soon vanish — approached not through nostalgia but through the strange ways memory changes once you've left a place behind.

This solo show, her first at LEESAYA, centers on a new video work rooted in the history of Hiroshima's Hiba region, her own hometown. The piece takes as its starting point a real event: Myoken-yama, a mountain adjoining Hibayama Goryo — traditionally identified in the Kojiki as the tomb of the goddess Izanami — was quarried, its stone used to build the Chugoku Expressway and other regional infrastructure. Yasuhara treats the breaking of a mythic mountain and its rebirth as roadway not as a rupture but as a continuous process of matter being broken down, transported, and given new form elsewhere — a road that, not incidentally, is also what let her leave home and later return to it.

The video combines documentary footage of the mountain, the quarry site and the expressway with animated sequences imagining Izanami's shattered body scattering into the land and reassembling as topography, layered with field-recorded sound — sirens, rockfall, blasting, passing traffic — that ties the mythological material back to the actual noise of ongoing land use. It's a quietly ambitious attempt to hold myth, geology, infrastructure and personal memory in the same frame.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 26, 5:00-7:00pm at Backyard (3-18-8 Shimomeguro, Meguro City)

shows.title: SHIN / RISE
shows.description:
Kanjiro Moriyama's solo show at A Lighthouse called Kanata brings together a suite of new sculptural works, all bearing variations on the title "Shin / Rise" — a play on the Japanese word for "stretching" or "extending upward." The pieces on view track a single sustained gesture across roughly a dozen works, made between 2024 and 2026, that appear to be studies in vertical growth and tension rather than a series of discrete, unrelated objects.

Moriyama's practice sits within a lineage of Japanese sculptors interested in material restraint — reducing form to essential lines and volumes so that surface, shadow and negative space carry as much weight as the material itself. Seeing the works together, numbered and sequenced like a single unfolding thought, is part of the point: the show invites a reading of sculpture as a kind of durational writing.

This is a compact, single-artist presentation in an intimate gallery space, well suited to close looking. The artist will be in the gallery for the opening days of the run, offering visitors a rare chance to talk through the work directly with him.

venue.name: A Lighthouse called Kanata
venue.about: A Lighthouse called Kanata is a contemporary art gallery in the Jingumae area of Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, near Omotesando Station. It was established in 2007 by Wahei Aoyama with the aim of introducing contemporary Japanese art and aesthetics to an international audience. The gallery's program centers on sculpture and painting by artists working within an emerging strand of Japanese aesthetics that reinstates beauty, technique, and materiality as central concerns, spanning media such as ceramics, glass, lacquer, metal, bamboo and wood alongside painting. The gallery frames its mission around a 'Return to Innocence' in contemporary art practice, positioning its roster of artists, many working in traditional craft mediums, within a global contemporary art context.

shows.title: DO NOT BOMB
shows.description:
"DO NOT BOMB" inaugurates NANZUKA's new flagship gallery in Shibuya Axsh with a solo exhibition devoted to the late Keiichi Tanaami (1936–2024), the pop artist whose garish, hallucinatory collages helped define postwar Japanese visual culture. The show is built around Tanaami's lifelong preoccupation with the memory of war — he was nine when Tokyo was firebombed in 1945 — tracing that thread from early 1960s silkscreens through to pieces he was still working on shortly before his death.

Expect the full range of Tanaami's vocabulary: dense collage-paintings that mix crushed glass, glitter and acrylic on canvas, silkscreen prints, and mixed-media sculpture, all cycling through his recurring imagery of spirals, cranes, elephants and anatomical diagrams lifted from historical medical illustration. One highlight, a large painting based on a 17th-century anatomical treatise, shows how Tanaami folded found and historical imagery into his own psychedelic, autobiographical universe.

Given that this is also the debut show for Nanzuka's new main space — stepping up from its longtime Underground location — there's an added charge to seeing a career-spanning tribute to one of the gallery's most closely identified artists mark the occasion.

venue.name: NANZUKA
venue.about: NANZUKA is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, founded by Shinji Nanzuka in 2005 in Shibuya as Nanzuka Underground, originally in a basement near Shibuya Crossing. The gallery focuses on rediscovering Japanese artists who were overlooked in the postwar fine-art scene, such as pop-art pioneer Keiichi Tanaami and airbrush illustrator Harumi Yamaguchi, while also promoting emerging Japanese talent and select international artists internationally. NANZUKA frequently collaborates with the fashion, music and design industries, expanding notions of what constitutes fine art. In 2021 it relocated its main space to a dedicated building in Harajuku and also runs satellite project spaces, Nanzuka 2G and 3110NZ. From 2013 to 2024 it operated a joint-venture branch in Hong Kong, AISHONANZUKA.

shows.title: Counting Myself II
shows.description:
Shiori Horie paints young female figures with an unnerving stillness — skin rendered in a cool, porcelain-like palette, expressions withheld rather than performed — that has made her one of the more closely watched figurative painters to come out of Japan's gallery scene in recent years. "Counting Myself II" continues a body of work she began with an earlier chapter of the same title, returning to the idea of self-accounting: painting as a way of tallying up who one is rather than presenting a finished self to the viewer.

The works on view lean into quiet, controlled compositions — solitary figures, restrained gesture, a sense of interior arithmetic playing out beneath a calm surface. Horie has shown at institutions including a solo presentation at Daiichi Seimei Gallery, and her paintings sit comfortably alongside a broader current of contemporary Japanese realism that treats the girl's portrait as a vessel for psychological inquiry rather than simple likeness.

This is one of two exhibitions opening at √K Contemporary in mid-September, running in the gallery's main space while a solo show by Sobin Park occupies its adjoining Space√K.

venue.name: √K Contemporary
venue.about: √K Contemporary is a contemporary art gallery in the Kagurazaka district of Tokyo, opened in March 2020 by SEI-RIN Co., Ltd., the company behind the long-established Japanese art dealer Kashima Arts. Its 300-square-metre space was designed around an 'outer space' concept, intended to present works with new values and perspectives. The gallery focuses on introducing a new generation of Japanese and international artists working across painting, photography, sculpture and new media, while situating their work within the broader lineage of Japanese art history. Below the main gallery, Space √K offers an industrial concrete basement rentable for exhibitions, fashion shows, and performances. The gallery regularly participates in major regional art fairs and has been featured in international art press.

shows.title: The Birth of Mir
shows.description:
Sobin Park works in pencil, bronze powder and drawing on silk engraving, building large panel works that read like fragments of invented myth. Figures and forms in "The Birth of Mir" hover somewhere between icon painting and comic-book panel, drawn with a fine, almost metallic line that catches light differently depending on where you stand — a direct result of the bronze powder worked into the graphite.

The exhibition continues a personal cosmology Park has been developing across recent bodies of work such as "The New Myth" and "The Dreaming," here narrowing in on a specific origin story of her own invention. The pieces are large-format — some spanning several meters across multiple panels — so the effect in the gallery is closer to standing before a mural or an altarpiece than looking at individual framed drawings.

The show occupies Space√K, the project space adjoining √K Contemporary's main gallery in Kagurazaka, where it runs alongside Shiori Horie's solo exhibition "Counting Myself II."

venue.name: √K Contemporary
venue.about: √K Contemporary is a contemporary art gallery in the Kagurazaka district of Tokyo, opened in March 2020 by SEI-RIN Co., Ltd., the company behind the long-established Japanese art dealer Kashima Arts. Its 300-square-metre space was designed around an 'outer space' concept, intended to present works with new values and perspectives. The gallery focuses on introducing a new generation of Japanese and international artists working across painting, photography, sculpture and new media, while situating their work within the broader lineage of Japanese art history. Below the main gallery, Space √K offers an industrial concrete basement rentable for exhibitions, fashion shows, and performances. The gallery regularly participates in major regional art fairs and has been featured in international art press.

shows.title: Wasaburo Itozono Exhibition — 25 Years After His Death
shows.description:
A quarter-century after his death, Mizoe Art Gallery is giving Wasaburo Itozono (1911–2001) a memorial exhibition drawn from the roughly one hundred of his works the gallery has quietly assembled over the years — around thirty paintings are on view here. Itozono trained under Kanji Maeda and moved through several of the independent-minded painting societies of mid-century Japan (the Dokuritsu Art Association, the Shinjin Gakai, the Free Art Association) before working on his own, later teaching at Nihon University's College of Art.

The paintings are quiet, observational things — gardens, birds, coastal towns, still lifes of pickled plums and camellias — built from simplified compositions that lean toward mood over description. It's the kind of unshowy, deeply schooled Japanese oil painting that rarely gets a spotlight outside specialist circles, which is exactly the gap this gallery has built its program around.

The show is accompanied by a talk on September 19th from Takayoshi Sakurai, a painter who studied under Itozono, reflecting on his teacher's working method and character — a rare chance to hear directly from someone who knew the artist, in the same rooms where his paintings now hang.
shows.reception: Talk event Saturday September 19 at 3pm with Takayoshi Sakurai, followed by a small reception

venue.name: Mizoe Art Gallery
venue.about: Mizoe Art Gallery was founded in Fukuoka in 2008 and opened a second space in Tokyo's Denenchofu neighborhood in 2012, linking the Kyushu and Tokyo art scenes and presenting Japanese art internationally. Both locations occupy detached houses set in large gardens in quiet residential areas; the Tokyo gallery is housed in a traditional Japanese-style residence where works are shown room by room. The gallery states its guiding concept as offering high-quality works and artists unaffected by trends or eras, favoring art of lasting, universal value. Its program spans modern and postwar Japanese painters and sculptors alongside major Western modern masters.
